items.q: Who is the source selection authority by default, and what team must the SSA establish?
items.a: The contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual. The SSA must establish an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition with contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise.

cite.quote: Agency heads are responsible for source selection. A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions.

items.q: Against what may competitive proposals be evaluated?
items.a: Solely the factors and subfactors stated in the RFP — nothing else.

cite.quote: Agencies must evaluate each competitive proposal based solely on the factors and subfactors in the RFP.

items.q: When is the tradeoff approach appropriate, and what must a higher-priced award show?
items.a: When it may be in the Government's best interest to award to other than the lowest-priced or highest-technically-rated offeror. It permits tradeoffs among price and non-price factors — but the anticipated benefits of the higher-priced proposal must merit the additional cost.

cite.quote: This process permits tradeoffs among cost or price and non-cost or non-price factors. The anticipated benefits of a higher priced proposal must merit the additional cost.

items.q: What defines the lowest price technically acceptable approach, and what does it forbid?
items.a: Award goes to the offeror with a technically acceptable proposal at the lowest evaluated price. It does not permit tradeoffs — technical superiority beyond acceptability buys nothing.

cite.quote: The lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) approach to source selection is appropriate when it is in the Government’s best interest to award to the offeror that submits a technically acceptable proposal with the lowest evaluated price. This approach does not permit tradeoffs.

items.q: How does the highest-technically-rated-with-a-fair-and-reasonable-price approach work?
items.a: All proposals are rated on the non-price factors; the highest technically rated proposal's price is then checked for fairness and reasonableness under subpart 15.4. If it fails, move to the next highest rated — no tradeoffs between price and non-price factors are considered.

cite.quote: The highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price approach to source selection is appropriate when the Government determines in advance that it would not be advantageous to consider tradeoffs between cost or price and non-cost or non-price factors; rather, the acquisition warrants paying any fair and reasonable price for the highest quality performance.

items.q: Must price or cost be evaluated in every competitive source selection?
items.a: Not always. For DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, the contracting officer may choose not to include price or cost as an award evaluation factor when the RFP is above the SAT, will result in multiple-award contracts for the same or similar services, and states the Government intends to award to each and all qualifying offerors — price or cost then must be considered on every order placed under the contract instead. Otherwise the baseline holds: price or cost in every competitive source selection, quality through one or more non-cost factors, and past performance unless the contracting officer documents why it is not appropriate.

cite.quote: for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard– (A) Contracting officers may choose not to include price or cost as an evaluation factor for award when an RFP– (1) Has an estimated value above the simplified acquisition threshold; (2) Will result in multiple-award contracts that are for the same or similar services; and (3) States that the Government intends to make an award to each and all qualifying offerors.

items.q: What must the RFP say about how non-price factors weigh against price?
items.a: At a minimum, whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when combined, are significantly more important than, approximately equal to, or significantly less important than cost or price.

cite.quote: whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when combined, are— (1) Significantly more important than cost or price; (2) Approximately equal to cost or price; or (3) Significantly less important than cost or price

items.q: What can clarifications never do?
items.a: Permit proposal revisions, cure deficiencies or material omissions, or materially alter the technical or cost elements of a proposal. They are discretionary — conducting clarifications with one offeror does not require them with any other.

cite.quote: Clarifications do not permit offerors to revise their proposal and cannot be used to cure proposal deficiencies or material omissions or materially alter the technical or cost elements of the proposal.

items.q: How do you evaluate an offeror with no relevant past performance record?
items.a: Neither favorably nor unfavorably — the absence of a record may not count for or against the offeror.

cite.quote: An offeror without a record of relevant past performance or for whom information on past performance is not available may not be evaluated favorably or unfavorably on past performance.

items.q: Define the competitive range. When is establishing one required?
items.a: The group of evaluated proposals the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. One must be established whenever negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals — and it may be limited to the greatest number that permits an efficient competition.

cite.quote: A competitive range is the group of evaluated proposals that the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. Contracting officers must establish a competitive range if negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals.

items.q: What is the minimum content of negotiations with each offeror in the competitive range?
items.a: Negotiate with each responsible offeror in the range, tailored to its proposal — and at a minimum indicate to, or negotiate with, each offeror any deficiencies or significant weaknesses in its proposal.

cite.quote: (i) Negotiate with each responsible offeror within the competitive range; and (ii) Tailor the negotiation to the offeror’s proposal, but at a minimum, indicate to, or negotiate with, each offeror any deficiencies or significant weaknesses in the proposal.

items.q: What happens when a proposal is eliminated from the competitive range?
items.a: No further revisions to that proposal can be accepted or considered. Elimination can happen at any time once the contracting officer concludes the offeror is unlikely to receive award, with written notice to the offeror.

cite.quote: (1) When a proposal is eliminated, no further revisions to the proposal can be accepted or considered. (2) Contracting officers may eliminate a proposal from the competitive range at any time upon concluding that the offeror is unlikely to receive an award.

items.q: When may a competitive award be made without negotiations?
items.a: When the RFP states the Government intends to evaluate proposals and make award without negotiation. If the Government then finds it necessary to negotiate anyway, the rationale must be documented in the contract file.

cite.quote: Contracting officers may make competitive awards without negotiations if the RFP states that the Government intends to evaluate proposals and make award without negotiation. If the RFP includes such a notice and the Government determines it is necessary to negotiate, the rationale for doing so must be documented in the contract file

items.q: What must the source selection decision document contain?
items.a: The SSA's independent judgment based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all RFP criteria, with the rationale for any business judgments and tradeoffs — including benefits associated with additional costs — though the tradeoffs need not be quantified.

cite.quote: The source selection decision must represent the SSA’s independent judgement and be based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all source selection criteria in the RFP. The source selection decision must be documented and include the rationale for any business judgments and tradeoffs made or relied on by the SSA, including benefits associated with additional costs. The documentation does not need to quantify the tradeoffs that led to the decision.

items.q: How quickly must an offeror request a postaward debriefing, and how soon should it occur?
items.a: The written request is due within 3 days after receipt of the award notice; the debriefing should occur within 5 days after receipt of the request, to the maximum extent practicable.

cite.quote: within 3 days after receipt of the award notice in accordance with 15.207-2. Such offerors must be debriefed and furnished the basis for the selection decision and contract award. (2) To the maximum extent practicable, the debriefing should occur within 5 days after receipt of the written request.

items.q: What must a postaward debriefing include?
items.a: The evaluation of significant weaknesses or deficiencies in the offeror's proposal; the overall evaluated cost or price and technical rating of both the successful and debriefed offerors, plus the debriefed offeror's past performance information; the overall ranking when one was developed; a summary of the award rationale; and reasonable responses to relevant procedural questions.

cite.quote: (i) The Government's evaluation of the significant weaknesses or deficiencies in the offeror's proposal, if applicable; (ii) The overall evaluated cost or price and technical rating of the successful offeror and the debriefed offeror, and past performance information on the debriefed offeror; (iii) The overall ranking of all offerors, when any ranking was developed by the agency during the source selection; (iv) A summary of the rationale for award

items.q: What must a postaward debriefing never include?
items.a: Point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with other offerors' proposals — or any information prohibited from disclosure, such as trade secrets, confidential cost breakdowns, or the names of past performance references.

cite.quote: The debriefing must not include point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with those of other offerors.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Above what dollar value must certified cost or pricing data be obtained?
items.a: For DoD: $10 million for prime contracts awarded after June 30, 2026, and $2.5 million for primes awarded on or before that date — R-DFARS 215.403-3(a), in lieu of the RFO baseline. Civilian agencies stayed at $2.5 million. Either way the duty yields to a 15.403-2 exception (DoD adds its own at 215.403-270), and a waiver remains worth requesting when the standards can be met.

cite.quote: In lieu of the requirements of FAR 15.403-3(a), obtain certified cost or pricing data when a prime contract is expected to exceed $10 million and is awarded after June 30, 2026, unless an exception at FAR 15.403-2 or DFARS 215.403-270 applies. The threshold is $2.5 million when the prime contract is awarded on or before June 30, 2026

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Name the exceptions that prohibit requiring certified cost or pricing data.
items.a: Adequate price competition; prices set by law or regulation; commercial products or services; an HCA waiver; and modifications of commercial-product or commercial-service contracts (plus the flat prohibition at or below the SAT).

cite.quote: (1) When the contracting officer determines that prices agreed upon are based on adequate price competition (see standards in paragraph (c)(1) of this subsection); (2) When the contracting officer determines that prices agreed upon are based on prices set by law or regulation (see standards in paragraph (c)(2) of this subsection); (3) When a commercial product or commercial service is being acquired (see standards in paragraph (c)(3) of this subsection); (4) When a waiver has been granted (see standards in paragraph (c)(4) of this subsection); or (5) When modifying a contract or subcontract for commercial products or commercial services

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Who can waive the certified cost or pricing data requirement?
items.a: The head of the contracting activity, without power of delegation, in exceptional cases — only if the price can be determined fair and reasonable without the data, with the authorization and rationale in writing.

cite.quote: In exceptional cases, the HCA may, without power of delegation, waive the requirement for submission of certified cost or pricing data if the price can be determined to be fair and reasonable without submission of certified cost or pricing data.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: A modification deletes $1.5 million of work and adds $1 million — a net $500,000 change. Does it cross the certified-data threshold?
items.a: Yes. Price adjustments count both increases and decreases, so this is a $2.5 million pricing adjustment that exceeds the threshold even though the net change is $500,000.

cite.quote: Price adjustment amounts must consider both increases and decreases ( e.g. , a $500,000 modification resulting from a reduction of $1,500,000 and an increase of $1,000,000 is a $2,500,000 pricing adjustment exceeding the $2,500,000 threshold).

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Which modifications never require certified cost or pricing data?
items.a: Modifications solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments, and exercising an option at the price established at award or initial negotiation.

cite.quote: Certified cost or pricing data are not required for modifications— (A) Solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments; or (B) To exercise an option at the price established at contract award or initial negotiation.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Does the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data guarantee the contractor's estimates, and does holding one excuse analysis?
items.a: No and no. The certificate applies to the facts the judgment was based on, not the accuracy of the contractor's judgment about future costs — and possession of a certificate is not a substitute for examining and analyzing the proposal.

cite.quote: The certificate does not constitute a representation as to the accuracy of the contractor's judgment on the estimate of future costs or projections. It applies to the data upon which the judgment or estimate was based.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: What is cost analysis?
items.a: The review and evaluation of separate cost elements and profit or fee in a proposal, applying judgment to determine how well the proposed costs represent what the contract should cost, assuming reasonable economy and efficiency.

cite.quote: Cost analysis is the review and evaluation of any separate cost elements and profit or fee in an offeror's or contractor's proposal, as needed to determine a fair and reasonable price or to determine cost realism, and the application of judgment to determine how well the proposed costs represent what the cost of the contract should be, assuming reasonable economy and efficiency.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: Define cost realism analysis.
items.a: Independently reviewing specific elements of each offeror's proposed cost estimate to determine whether they are realistic for the work, reflect a clear understanding of the requirements, and are consistent with the offeror's own technical proposal.

cite.quote: Cost realism analysis is the process of independently reviewing and evaluating specific elements of each offeror's proposed cost estimate to determine whether the estimated proposed cost elements are realistic for the work to be performed; reflect a clear understanding of the requirements; and are consistent with the unique methods of performance and materials described in the offeror's technical proposal.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: On which contracts is cost realism analysis mandatory, and what number does it produce?
items.a: On cost-reimbursement contracts — it determines each offeror's probable cost of performance, which may differ from the proposed cost and must be used for the best-value evaluation.

cite.quote: Cost realism analyses must be performed on cost-reimbursement contacts to determine the probable cost of performance for each offeror.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: May offered prices be adjusted when cost realism is applied to competitive fixed-price proposals?
items.a: No. Realism results may inform performance-risk assessments and responsibility determinations, but proposals are evaluated on the RFP criteria and the offered prices must not be adjusted.

cite.quote: However, proposals must be evaluated using the criteria in the RFP, and the offered prices must not be adjusted as a result of the analysis.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: What is unbalanced pricing, and what may it cost an offeror?
items.a: Despite an acceptable total evaluated price, one or more line items are significantly over- or understated. The risks must be considered in the competitive range and the selection decision — and the offer may be rejected if the imbalance poses an unacceptable risk.

cite.quote: Unbalanced pricing exists when, despite an acceptable total evaluated price, the price of one or more line items is significantly over or understated as indicated by the application of cost or price analysis techniques.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: What is the Government entitled to when certified cost or pricing data prove defective after award?
items.a: A price adjustment, including profit or fee, of any significant amount by which the price was increased because of the inaccurate, incomplete, or noncurrent data — plus recovery of overpayments with interest, and penalties for knowing submissions.

cite.quote: the Government is entitled to a price adjustment, including profit or fee, of any significant amount by which the price was increased because of the defective data.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: What are the statutory cost-plus-fixed-fee ceilings?
items.a: 15 percent of estimated cost for experimental, developmental, or research work; 10 percent for all other CPFF contracts; and for architect-engineer services, 6 percent of the estimated construction cost — but that 6 percent is the civilian baseline. For the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, R-DFARS 236.202-371 sets the A-E design-fee limit at 10 percent.

cite.quote: (i) For experimental, developmental, or research work performed under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, the fee must not exceed 15 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee. (ii) For architect-engineer services for public works or utilities, the contract price or the estimated cost and fee for production and delivery of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications must not exceed 6 percent of the estimated cost of construction of the public work or utility, excluding fees. (iii) For other cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, the fee must not exceed 10 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: What is the architect-engineer design-fee limit for the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force?
items.a: 10 percent of the project's estimated construction cost — the military departments' statutory limit under R-DFARS 236.202-371, which displaces the 6 percent civilian baseline. It reaches modifications and redesign work too, but only the portion of the price attributable to preparing designs, plans, drawings, and specifications.

cite.quote: The statutes at 10 U.S.C. 7540, 8612, and 9540, for the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force, respectively, limit the contract price (or fee) for architect-engineer services for the preparation of designs, plans, drawings, and specifications to 10 percent of the project's estimated construction cost.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: May you settle the fee first and negotiate cost later?
items.a: No. Profit or fee is one of several interrelated variables — the contracting officer must not agree on profit or fee without concurrent agreement on cost and contract type. At a true impasse, refer the action to a level above the contracting officer.

cite.quote: Because profit or fee is only one of several interrelated variables, contracting officers must not agree on profit or fee without concurrent agreement on cost and type of contract.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: May another contract's prices or profits influence this negotiation?
items.a: No. Each contract is priced separately and independently — no proposed price reductions under other contracts, no losses or profits realized or anticipated elsewhere, and no contingency amounts the contract already covers by adjustment.

cite.quote: Contracting officers must price each contract separately and independently and not— (1) Consider proposed price reductions under other contracts; (2) Consider losses or profits realized or anticipated under other contracts

items.q: What happens when responsibility cannot be clearly established?
items.a: No award — a contract requires an affirmative determination of responsibility, and without a clear indication of responsibility the contracting officer must determine the offeror nonresponsible. The prospective contractor bears the burden of affirmatively demonstrating its responsibility.

cite.quote: Do not award a contract award before making an affirmative determination of contractor responsibility. Without a clear indication of responsibility, make a determination of nonresponsibility.

items.q: Recite the general standards of responsibility.
items.a: Adequate financial resources (or the ability to obtain them); ability to meet the delivery or performance schedule given existing commitments; a satisfactory performance record; a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; the necessary organization, experience, controls, and technical skills; the necessary production, construction, and technical equipment and facilities; and being otherwise qualified and eligible under applicable laws.

cite.quote: (a) Have adequate financial resources to perform the contract, or the ability to obtain them (see 9.104-3(a)); (b) Be able to comply with the required or proposed delivery or performance schedule, taking into consideration all existing commercial and governmental business commitments; (c) Have a satisfactory performance record

items.q: What integrity database check precedes award above the SAT?
items.a: Review the performance and integrity information in FAPIIS — including SAM exclusions and CPARS — and document in the file how it was considered in the responsibility determination.

cite.quote: Before awarding a contract exceeding the simplified acquisition threshold, review the performance and integrity information available in the Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System (FAPIIS)

items.q: What two principles underlie the organizational conflict of interest rules?
items.a: Preventing conflicting roles that might bias a contractor's judgment, and preventing unfair competitive advantage.

cite.quote: The two underlying principles are— (a) Preventing the existence of conflicting roles that might bias a contractor’s judgment; and (b) Preventing unfair competitive advantage.

items.q: What are the contracting officer's OCI duties?
items.a: Identify and evaluate potential conflicts as early in the acquisition process as possible, and avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before contract award — recommending a course of action to the HCA before issuing a solicitation that may involve a significant conflict.

cite.quote: (1) Identify and evaluate potential organizational conflicts of interest as early in the acquisition process as possible; and (2) Avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before contract award.

items.q: Who approves an OCI waiver, and how far may that authority be delegated?
items.a: The agency head or a designee, on a written request setting forth the extent of the conflict — and the authority must not be delegated below the head of a contracting activity.

cite.quote: Any request for waiver must be in writing, must set forth the extent of the conflict, and requires approval by the agency head or a designee. Agency heads must not delegate waiver authority below the level of head of a contracting activity.

items.q: When does an unfair competitive advantage exist?
items.a: When a competing contractor possesses proprietary information obtained from a Government official without proper authorization, or source selection information relevant to the contract that is not available to all competitors and would assist it in winning.

cite.quote: an unfair competitive advantage exists where a contractor competing for award of any Federal contract possesses- (1) Proprietary information that was obtained from a Government official without proper authorization; or (2) Source selection information (as defined in 2.101) that is relevant to the contract but is not available to all competitors, and such information would assist that contractor in obtaining the contract.

items.q: What two categories of information does the procurement integrity rule protect from disclosure?
items.a: Contractor bid or proposal information and source selection information — neither may be disclosed to anyone not authorized to receive it.

cite.quote: No person or entity may disclose contractor bid or proposal information or source selection information to any person other than those authorized to receive that information

items.q: Where does a procurement integrity violation go if it impacts the procurement?
items.a: To the head of the contracting activity. The contracting officer first determines whether the violation affects the pending award or selection; if it does, all information goes promptly to the HCA, who decides what happens next.

cite.quote: (2) If the contracting officer determines the violation does impact the procurement, the contracting officer must promptly forward all information to the HCA.

items.q: What can the HCA direct before award if a procurement integrity violation is confirmed?
items.a: Cancel the procurement, disqualify an offeror, or take other appropriate actions to protect the Government's interests.

cite.quote: (1) If a contract has not been awarded— (i) Cancel the procurement; (ii) Disqualify an offeror; or (iii) Take other appropriate actions to protect Government interests.

items.q: State the GAO postaward stay rule precisely.
items.a: If the agency receives GAO's protest notice within 10 days after award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered under a required debriefing — whichever is later — the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance or terminate the contract, unless the HCA authorizes continued performance.

cite.quote: If the agency receives notice of a protest from the GAO within 10 days after contract award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered to the protester for any debriefing that is required by 15.505 or 15.506, whichever is later, then the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance or terminate the awarded contract, unless the head of the contracting activity authorizes contract performance.

items.q: Who can override a GAO protest stay, and on what bases?
items.a: The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, upon a written finding that performance is in the best interests of the United States, or that urgent and compelling circumstances significantly affecting U.S. interests will not permit waiting for GAO's decision — and GAO must be notified before performance is authorized.

cite.quote: The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, may authorize contract performance, upon a written finding that— (i) Contract performance will be in the best interests of the United States; or (ii) Urgent and compelling circumstances that significantly affect the interests of the United States will not permit waiting for the GAO's decision.
